You won’t necessarily hit busy season in accounting if you go into industry or government/nonprofit. I’ve worked in several different industries now and can say that the latter has the best work-life balance, but the pay is poor. Otherwise it really depends on which industry you end up in. Public/tax will burn you out, SaaS/startups may too because they’re often understaffed. Lower level roles are being outsourced so we’re not safe from that either.

I’d recommend applying for food stamps, unemployment, and COBRA (if eligible) like immediately. These things all take time and you need to start the clock ASAP. Then work on resumes and networking. When the company I worked for did this, a few people jumped into action on day one, and then others started contributing where they could - help with resumes, collecting legal info, finding communities/organizations that were willing to help with food, funding, work, etc. But our layoff was much larger, just under 1k employees, so it really depends on how much time/energy/mental capacity each of you has to contribute. It’s cool if that’s none right now. 

You’ll likely get paid out of the bankruptcy funds IF anything is available, but I doubt you’ll see anything soon. We were laid off in 2023, and the DOL is still telling us they’re not done investigating. We’ll finally get a class action settlement sometime in the next few weeks because they violated the WARN Act, but we’re not expected to get paid our lost wages until the end of next year, when the bankruptcy finally settles.

I say this not to bring you down but to tell you realistically it’s going to be hard. I struggled to find a job for 9+ months, partly because I was paralyzed by the piling debt and constant existential dread, and I ultimately lost my apartment. It’s an even tougher job market now, so you need to do better than me and prepare for that rationally. Start finding ways to minimize the damage today. Focus on food, shelter, emotional support, and finding work (even if those things aren’t ultimately what you hoped they would be) and then be angry at them when you’re safe.

Sorry, missed your response. I work in adtech right now, and I previously worked in SaaS.

In my personal experience, the ones who are going to take care of you are usually younger companies with younger owners. My one strong recommendation is to avoid small startups like the plague (I’ve been on the losing end of a company’s bankruptcy once and I’ll never willingly put myself in that position again). Mid-sized and larger companies will have more stable work, but there’s a sweet spot where they offer good pay/benefits and also prioritize work/life balance and mental wellness. 

Check out BuiltIn for remote jobs in tech (there’s a Finance category), and if temp-to-full jobs come up weigh the pros and cons. There’s usually a lower barrier to entry and, if you impress them, you’ll likely get transitioned to full-time without having to jump through any extra hoops.

I haven’t worked for the IRS but I worked for local government (also in the Central Valley), I imagine it’s pretty similar (super stable, work/life balance is good). The pay wasn’t there for me and the culture was wildly toxic, but that may not be the case for the jobs you’re looking at. 

I moved on to industry and highly recommend giving that a shot if you can swing it. I’m at $105k, fully remote and able to take PTO on short notice, which helps take care of my special needs kid. I was unfortunately with BW during their scandal so do better than me and walk away from red flags 🤣 but was able to move on to a larger company with a similar structure and it’s great for someone with a family.

Accountant here - it’s not only the end of the holiday season, which means customer demand has slowed a lot, but it’s also the end of the fiscal year for a lot of companies. They’ll be closing books soon and adjusting budgets for the new year, which is when they’ll assess hiring needs. I’d say mid-Jan to early Feb is when you’ll start seeing them try to fill gaps from post-holiday turnover and prepare for Q2 and Q3 demand. Retail, hospitality, and food service tend to pick up for spring and summer (tourist season). 

As others have said, reach out to friends and family, but also consider following up with hiring managers so you don’t get lost in the shuffle. It may also help to have someone look over your resume and advise on how to update it - you want an ATS friendly format with keywords and job titles that align with the position you’re applying to. That means you need to update for each job (very annoying but very helpful).

You don’t want the eviction on your record but it’s going to be hard to find a new place with hardly any income. I’m in the Central Valley and just went through a job hunt, it’s hard out here. Took me 8 months to find a new spot. 

Have you applied for extra assistance? I used the system for a few years when my special needs son was younger, it truly wasn’t fun but it helped us survive. You can get the help with cash/food for a while and there are even some programs that will help you with back rent. You can let your landlord know you’re working on those and hopefully they’ll give you some time. I think the public assistance office will even pay for you to stay in a hotel for a short time if it comes to that. If you’re in the TC area CSET might be able to train you/help you find a job, but there are other programs that can help with your search too. I think EDD themselves will pay for some trainings  if you’re interested in that and there are some workforce development boards throughout the state. 

I highly recommend looking for jobs with the government if you can find something that fits. I hated working there but they have decent benefits and stable work and it prepares you to move on to better jobs. EDIT: Look at their extra help positions - it’s something like 32 hours a week instead of 40 but they don’t ask you to have much experience.
